title: Imbalances are a feature of the global financial system, not a bug
gist: Global imbalances — a US net external liability of 70 per cent of GDP, China's goods surplus, Europe's savings outflow — are the arithmetic sum of domestic saving/investment choices, not a global pathology, and the US dollar's currency mismatch (dollar liabilities, foreign-currency assets) makes the US external position self-stabilizing rather than crisis-prone. The real signal is domestic: US gross government debt near 125 per cent of GDP with rising Treasury yields, European under-investment pushing savings into US AI, and Chinese over-investment suppressing consumption. The G7 and G20 failure to act means policymakers are using 'global imbalances' as a smokescreen and reaching for poorly targeted tools like tariffs.

insights.claim: Cross-border financial imbalances are the arithmetic sum of each country's domestic saving-investment gaps rather than a distinct global phenomenon, so diagnosing them as an international problem misidentifies the cause.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frame any policy response to imbalances as a domestic-fiscal/structural trade rather than an FX or trade-agreement trade; international communiqués will not move the underlying flows.
insights.quote: In truth, ‘global imbalances’ are not primarily a global phenomenon. They are simply the product of all the world’s domestic imbalances added up.
insights.locator: In truth, 'global imbalances' are not

insights.claim: Capital-account openness delivers international risk-sharing as its primary benefit, letting non-domestic investors diversify away from sluggish home assets while domestic residents avoid bearing all the risk of their own economy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat rising external liabilities in an outperforming economy as a symptom of investable opportunity, not distress — the opposite of the standard EM-crisis read.
insights.quote: This is textbook, win-win international risk-sharing.
insights.locator: The world has open capital accounts to diversify risk

insights.claim: Sharing risk and eliminating risk are distinct: openness redistributes exposure across borders but does not reduce it, and the cost is that overseas investors are 'flightier' because they lack home bias, have no stake in domestic politics, and doubt legal protection as foreign nationals.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Foreign ownership share is the variable to track for drawdown speed in any asset class — high foreign ownership means faster, more discontinuous repricing on a policy shock.
insights.quote: Sharing risk and eliminating risk are not the same thing.
insights.locator: No free lunches

insights.claim: Because foreign capital is more mobile than domestic capital, it punishes bad domestic policymaking faster by relocating, which imposes real constraints on political choices and lowers the likelihood of bad policy being enacted.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Capital flight is a disciplining mechanism, so watch flow reversals as a leading indicator that a government is about to be forced into reform — often ahead of the policy announcement itself.
insights.locator: And because foreign investment is more mobile than domestic investment

insights.claim: The US net liability to the world — the degree to which its overseas borrowing exceeds its overseas investments — reached 70 per cent of US GDP in 2025, far outstripping the largest surpluses elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Anchor number for any imbalance debate: the headline is alarming enough to drive policy noise even though the author argues the position is robust.
insights.quote: The US’s net liability to the world – the degree to which its overseas borrowing exceeds its overseas investments – reached an astonishing 70 per cent of US GDP in 2025.
insights.locator: Seemingly this focus on global imbalances is justified

insights.claim: The US external position is self-correcting because its liabilities are denominated in dollars while its assets are in foreign currency: a rebalancing away from the US weakens the dollar, which raises the dollar value of US external assets and stabilizes the net position.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A dollar sell-off mechanically improves the US net international investment position, so expect valuation effects — not a funding crisis — as the adjustment channel; positions betting on a US external funding break are fighting this arithmetic.
insights.quote: US liabilities are in dollars. Its assets are in foreign currency. So, if investors rebalance away from the US, the dollar depreciates. That raises the (dollar) value of US external assets, stabilizing the overall external position.
insights.locator: Even today’s huge US net liability looks robust

insights.claim: US Treasuries attract global savings because they are safe, backed by a huge economy and the rule of law, and highly liquid, which makes reserve-asset issuance a structural driver of the US deficit rather than a policy failure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The rule-of-law and liquidity premium is the load-bearing assumption in the Treasury bid — erosion of either, not deficit size alone, is what would break demand.
insights.locator: First, the US issues the world’s reserve asset, US Treasuries

insights.claim: US outperformance driven by its tech boom means domestic investment opportunities exceed domestic saving, so foreign capital inflows reflect opportunity rather than a nefarious 'transfer of wealth' out of the US.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If US tech-driven returns fade, the inflow rationale weakens simultaneously with the growth story — the two are the same trade, not a hedge pair.
insights.quote: Put simply, investment opportunities in the US outstrip US saving.
insights.locator: Second, the US economy has outperformed the rest of the world

insights.claim: Current imbalance levels are the most prominent since just before the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, but a rerun is not in prospect because that crisis was caused by lax financial standards in Europe and the US, not by the 'Global Savings Glut'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not use imbalance size as a crisis-timing indicator; the variable that actually predicts a break is financial-regulatory laxity, which is a separate thing to monitor.
insights.quote: That crisis was caused by lax financial standards in Europe and the US, not the fabled ‘ Global Savings Glut ’.
insights.locator: Do these flighty investors and global imbalances presage a rerun

insights.claim: Imbalances are not an imminent risk in themselves but function as a credible early warning signal of domestic problems, making them a diagnostic instrument rather than a hazard to be neutralized.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Read the current-account print as a read-through to a country's fiscal and structural policy quality, and position on the domestic reform trajectory it implies.
insights.quote: Global imbalances are not in themselves an imminent risk. Rather, they are a credible early warning signal of domestic problems.
insights.locator: Global imbalances are not in themselves an imminent risk

insights.claim: The claims that imports steal jobs and that a reserve-currency issuer must run deficits are described as easily falsified, yet both are seductive enough to shape political discourse and drive policy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect policy built on these premises regardless of their validity — the trade is on the policy, not on the economics being right.
insights.quote: easily falsified claims that imports steal jobs, or that a reserve currency issuer must run deficits
insights.locator: To the untrained ear ‘global’ imbalances sound like a global problem

themes.theme: Three domestic policy failures: US fiscal, EU investment, China consumption

insights.claim: US gross government debt at nearly 125 per cent of GDP exceeds the entirety of what the US collectively owes the rest of the world, making the fiscal position a larger problem than the external position.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The domestic debt stock, not the external balance, is the binding constraint to watch for US rates — a useful reframe when imbalance headlines dominate.
insights.quote: At nearly 125 per cent of GDP, the US government’s gross debt is greater than the US’s entire external liabilities (or what it collectively owes the world).
insights.locator: The US government, for instance, spends too much borrowed money

insights.claim: Rising US Treasury yields are already prompting 'exotic policy responses' and putting pressure on an unsustainable US fiscal position.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for unconventional fiscal-financing measures as yields rise; the phrase 'exotic policy responses' flags tail-risk policy actions that would reprice duration and the dollar.
insights.quote: US Treasury yields have been rising, prompting exotic policy responses and putting pressure on the unsustainable US fiscal position.
insights.locator: US Treasury yields have been rising

insights.claim: Europe's failure to create domestic investment opportunities is pushing its savings toward higher returns abroad, specifically into US AI investment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: European savings are a structural marginal bid for the US AI capex complex; any EU policy that successfully creates domestic investment opportunities would remove part of that bid.
insights.quote: Europeans, meanwhile, aren’t creating investment opportunities. Their savings are therefore flowing to where returns are more attractive – especially US AI investment.
insights.locator: Europeans, meanwhile, aren’t creating investment opportunities

insights.claim: Europe's lack of investment has allowed competitiveness to erode, leaving it falling further behind the US and vulnerable to Chinese competition — a compounding dynamic where the savings outflow worsens the gap that caused it.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Second-order: the Europe-underperformance trade is self-reinforcing until a domestic investment regime change, so relative-value shorts on European competitiveness have a long runway.
insights.locator: That lack of investment has allowed competitiveness to erode

insights.claim: China funnels excess savings into excessive investment, which inflates asset bubbles and depresses consumption, and after its housing bubble collapsed exports surged while domestic demand including import demand stayed feeble.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China's export surge is a symptom of suppressed domestic demand, so expect continued surplus and continued trading-partner backlash until Chinese consumption policy changes.
insights.quote: It funnels its savings into excessive investment, inflating asset bubbles and depressing consumption.
insights.locator: At the same time, China spends too little

insights.claim: China's goods trade surplus now alarms Europe's leaders as much as it worries America's, broadening the coalition of economies with a grievance against Chinese export policy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Trade-defence measures against China are likely to come from both sides of the Atlantic, not just Washington — widen the exposure map beyond US tariff risk.
insights.locator: China’s trade in goods surplus now alarms Europe’s leaders

insights.claim: In each of the US, European and Chinese cases the appropriate domestic policy prescription is obvious but the political will to enact it is lacking.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Base case is persistence of the current configuration — imbalances widen rather than correct, so mean-reversion trades on current-account gaps lack a catalyst.
insights.quote: In each case the appropriate domestic policy prescription is obvious – but the political will is lacking.
insights.locator: In each case the appropriate domestic policy prescription

themes.theme: G7/G20 coordination failure and the tariff smokescreen

insights.claim: The G7 failed to agree either fiscal consolidation in the US or accelerated structural reform in Europe and instead punted the issue to August's G20 finance ministers' summit, which then failed to produce a communiqué at all.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that coordinated adjustment is off the table; price multilateral policy risk as noise rather than as a driver of flows.
insights.quote: rather than leading by example, the G7 failed to agree either fiscal consolidation in the US or accelerated structural reform in Europe
insights.locator: And recent international meetings confirm

insights.claim: The language in the G20 chair's statement was noticeably tougher on surplus countries than on deficit countries, and the US openly blamed China for the failure to reach agreement.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The asymmetric framing signals that surplus economies will bear the adjustment demands — raises the probability of further measures aimed at Chinese and other surplus exporters.
insights.quote: The language that emerged in the ‘chair’s statement’ was noticeably tougher on surplus countries than on deficit countries.
insights.locator: The language that emerged in the ‘chair’s statement’

insights.claim: Tariffs are characterized as poorly targeted policy that does nothing to address the underlying saving-investment causes of imbalances, making them politically attractive but economically inert on the stated problem.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Do not expect tariffs to narrow the deficits they are justified by; model them purely as a cost shock and a trade-relations variable.
insights.quote: And it can be seen in poorly targeted policies like tariffs, which do nothing to address the underlying issues.
insights.locator: And it can be seen in poorly targeted policies like tariffs

insights.claim: Some governments are attempting to dress up domestic policy failings as the result of foreign actions, and the emphasis on the 'global' dimension without credible follow-through risks undermining rather than advancing the case for difficult domestic reform.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Each round of global-imbalance rhetoric lowers the odds of the domestic reforms that would actually fix the flows — a negative feedback loop for anyone waiting on fiscal or structural adjustment.
insights.quote: The current focus on ‘global imbalances’ is too easily used by policymakers as a smokescreen for their own domestic failings.
insights.locator: Expert comment, opening line

insights.claim: Hélène Rey's argument is that linking individual national challenges could surface a broad common interest enabling simultaneous action, where US fiscal consolidation is offset by rising European investment and Chinese consumption, easing both the economics and the politics of adjustment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The only benign path out of the current configuration requires synchronized policy across three blocs — a low-probability scenario worth pricing as a tail, not a base case.
insights.quote: Any fiscal consolidation enacted by the US, for instance, could be offset by rising investment in Europe and consumption in China.
insights.locator: Stones and glasshouses

insights.claim: The unfashionable Washington Consensus rule that prosperity comes from putting your own house in order rather than casting stones at neighbours is invoked as the correct prescription for today's imbalance debate.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals an intellectual rehabilitation of domestic-reform orthodoxy at a major policy institute — watch for that framing to resurface in official commentary.
insights.quote: As the unfashionable Washington Consensus used to have it, the key to prosperity is putting your own house in order, not casting stones at your neighbours.
insights.locator: As the unfashionable Washington Consensus used to have it
